State governments across Australia have expanded borrowing significantly — infrastructure pipelines, housing commitments, post-pandemic spending. ideas.title: Asset Recycling: Africa's Underused Infrastructure Funding Lever
ideas.context: African Business argues that asset recycling — governments monetising existing infrastructure to fund new builds — remains structurally underused across Africa despite its proven track record in Australia and parts of Asia. The AfDB's $15 million targeted investment into North Africa companies confirms that development finance institutions are actively seeking catalytic mechanisms to crowd in private capital, which is precisely the gap asset recycling is designed to fill. The tension is that AfDB-style grants address early-stage companies, while asset recycling targets mature public assets — together they represent complementary but still disconnected parts of the capital stack.
ideas.angle: Asset recycling could unlock Africa's infrastructure backlog without waiting for new public budget allocations — but it requires regulatory frameworks that most African governments have yet to build.

linkedin_playbook.opening_hook: Australia used asset recycling to fund billions in new infrastructure. Africa has the assets. So why isn't the model travelling?
linkedin_playbook.why_section: Africa faces an infrastructure financing gap estimated in the hundreds of billions annually. Traditional ODA and DFI grants are necessary but insufficient. Asset recycling — leasing or selling mature state-owned assets to private operators and ringfencing proceeds for new infrastructure — offers a self-funding loop that doesn't depend on aid cycles or sovereign debt headroom. The AfDB's renewed focus on private sector catalysis in North Africa signals that the continent's premier development bank is looking beyond grants. The missing piece is the enabling legislation and transaction advisory capacity at the national level.
linkedin_playbook.unique_take: The conversation in Africa tends to conflate privatisation with asset recycling — they are not the same. Recycling preserves long-term public ownership intent while releasing near-term capital. Australia's model worked because it separated the transaction from the politics of ownership. African governments that can make that distinction clearly will move faster and attract better-quality institutional investors.

pages.markdown:
**Australia used asset recycling to fund billions in new infrastructure. Africa has the assets. So why isn't the model travelling?**

Asset recycling is not privatisation. It's a funding mechanism: governments lease or sell mature public assets to private operators, then ringfence the proceeds to build new infrastructure. The ownership intent stays public. The capital moves now.

African Business recently examined why this model — proven in Australia and parts of Southeast Asia — remains structurally underused across Africa. The diagnosis is familiar: weak enabling legislation, limited transaction advisory capacity, and a political conflation of recycling with sell-offs.

Meanwhile, the AfDB is deploying $15 million to catalyse private investment in North African companies — a signal that Africa's premier development bank is actively looking for mechanisms beyond grants to crowd in institutional capital. Asset recycling fits that mandate precisely.

The gap isn't appetite. Sovereign wealth funds, infrastructure funds, and pension capital are actively seeking long-duration African assets. The gap is the transaction architecture — the legal frameworks, independent regulators, and ringfencing rules that give investors confidence the proceeds won't be absorbed into general revenue.

Australia's model worked because it separated the transaction from the politics of ownership. African governments that can make that distinction clearly — and communicate it — will access a deeper pool of capital than any grant cycle can provide.

The infrastructure backlog won't close on aid alone. Asset recycling is one of the few mechanisms that can generate a self-funding loop.

**Which African market do you think is closest to executing a credible asset recycling transaction — and what's the single biggest barrier holding it back?**

**Everyone credits Israel's startup success to venture capital and government R&D grants. The real engine is a military alumni network most outsiders never examine.**

The IDF's Unit 8200 Alumni Association doesn't just connect former intelligence officers — it actively orchestrates the conversion of military-grade technical training into civilian startup output. Structured matching, deliberate co-founder introductions, and a shared trust architecture that dramatically lowers the friction of early-stage company building.

The result: a disproportionate share of Israel's most successful technology companies trace their founding teams back to this single network.

Here's what the consensus misses: the capital came *after* the network density was established, not before. Investors followed the deal flow that the alumni association was already generating internally.

Now consider Africa. The AfDB is deploying $15 million to catalyse North African tech companies — welcome, necessary capital. But capital without network infrastructure produces isolated winners. It doesn't produce ecosystems.

Africa has the raw ingredients: world-class engineering graduates, a growing diaspora with global experience, and government programmes beginning to take innovation seriously. What's missing is the structured alumni layer — the association, the cohort, the trusted network that converts individual talent into coordinated startup output.

Diaspora capital (which Nigeria's President Tinubu is actively courting) and diaspora talent networks are different instruments. Both matter. But the network comes first.

The risk of getting this wrong: Africa continues to produce individual unicorns without building the ecosystem density that makes the next generation of founders cheaper and faster to back.

For investors and operators working across southern Africa, the practical implication is this: financial reform progress should be measured not just by banking sector health indicators, but by whether domestic capital markets are deepening fast enough to intermediate the long-term investment the region needs.

The reform lever that gets pulled first matters enormously for sequencing. Get it wrong and you spend a decade stabilising banks while the real constraint — shallow markets — goes unaddressed.

pages.markdown:
**Five years ago, Togo's economy ran on motorcycle taxis and cash. Today, it's one of West Africa's most cited examples of digital financial transformation. What actually changed — and what can other markets learn from it?**

**The challenge:** Togo had a large, active informal economy with minimal formal financial infrastructure. Banking penetration was low. Credit bureaus were thin. The formal reform agenda was slow.

**The turning point:** Mobile money didn't wait for the formal system to catch up. It met informal economic activity — the zemidjans, the market traders, the remittance flows — exactly where that activity already existed. Transaction data accumulated. Digital identity followed. Credit products emerged from the data, not from a top-down banking reform.

**The outcome:** A digitally intermediated financial economy that leapfrogged the traditional sequencing. Formal institutions are now adapting around the data and transaction infrastructure that mobile money created — not the other way around.

This matters beyond Togo's borders. Nelson Mandela University's recent analysis of southern Africa's financial reform agenda focuses on the formal architecture: banking regulation, exchange rate management, capital market depth. All necessary. All slow.

Togo's trajectory suggests a parallel path — one where informal economic density, mobile penetration, and fintech product design do the work that formal reform struggles to do quickly.

For investors and operators: markets with high informal economic activity and strong mobile penetration may be closer to financial inclusion scale than their formal sector indicators suggest. Togo is the proof of concept.
